blocks.content: Every DNS based lookup mentioned so far in this module has been resolved by one specific component, referenced only briefly until now. This topic gives CoreDNS, the engine underneath every Service name resolution, its own complete treatment.
DNS, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: DNS, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: Kubernetes runs its own internal DNS service, most commonly implemented by a project called CoreDNS, deployed as a set of Pods running inside the cluster itself, just like any other application workload.

CoreDNS watches the API server continuously for Service and Pod changes and automatically maintains a live, always current mapping of names to addresses, requiring no manual DNS record management from any engineer.

Every Pod in the cluster is automatically configured, through its container's resolv.conf file, to send DNS queries to CoreDNS by default, which is precisely why calling a Service by its short name simply works without extra setup.

CoreDNS is not an optional add on in a properly functioning cluster. It is a core, foundational piece of infrastructure, and its own health directly determines whether service discovery works at all across the entire cluster.

blocks.content: Running As Its Own Dedicated Cluster Workload
blocks.text: Running As Its Own Dedicated Cluster Workload

blocks.content: CoreDNS itself runs as a Deployment inside the kube-system namespace, meaning it is deployed, scaled, and monitored using exactly the same Kubernetes primitives already covered throughout this course, including Deployments and Services.

This is a genuinely elegant piece of design: the component responsible for making every other Service discoverable is itself just another Deployment behind its own Service, using the very system it provides discovery for.

Because CoreDNS runs as ordinary Pods, it benefits from all the same resilience already covered in earlier modules. If a CoreDNS Pod fails, the ReplicaSet controlling it creates a replacement automatically, exactly as covered in Module 5.

Running kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns shows the actual CoreDNS Pods currently running in the cluster, making this normally invisible piece of infrastructure directly visible and inspectable.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784642050712-78196505.png
blocks.alt: CoreDNS running as its own dedicated cluster workload

blocks.content: A Real DNS Resolution Example

Consider the backend-service name used throughout the previous topic. When a frontend Pod's code resolves that name, the actual DNS query sent is for the short name, which the Pod's resolv.conf search domains automatically expand.

That expansion appends the calling Pod's own namespace and the cluster's domain suffix, producing a fully qualified name such as backend-service.default.svc.cluster.local, which CoreDNS then resolves to the Service's cluster IP.

This automatic expansion through search domains is exactly why application code can use the short, clean name backend-service in the overwhelming majority of cases, without ever needing to type out the full, verbose qualified form.

Running kubectl exec into any Pod and then running nslookup backend-service.default.svc.cluster.local shows this full resolution chain directly, confirming exactly how CoreDNS is answering the query end to end.

$ kubectl exec -it frontend-pod -- nslookup backend-service
Server:    10.96.0.10
Address:   10.96.0.10:53

Name:      backend-service.default.svc.cluster.local
Address:   10.96.14.201

blocks.content: The previous topic introduced DNS based discovery as the strongly preferred of the two service discovery mechanisms, but deliberately left the precise mechanics of how that DNS resolution actually happens for this dedicated topic.

Every claim made in that previous topic, that DNS lookups happen fresh on demand, that they always reflect the cluster's current state, is now fully explained by CoreDNS continuously watching the API server for live changes.

This is the same building pattern already used repeatedly across this module: introduce a concept briefly where it is first needed, then return to it later with the complete, dedicated depth it deserves once the surrounding context has been established.

With this topic's depth now in place, the entire service discovery story from the beginning of this module through here should feel like one connected, complete mechanism rather than a series of separate, unrelated facts.

blocks.content: The Predictable Naming Convention

Every Service created in a Kubernetes cluster automatically receives a fully qualified DNS name following the exact pattern service-name.namespace-name.svc.cluster.local, with no manual configuration required to establish this mapping.

The svc segment in that pattern specifically indicates the name refers to a Service object, distinguishing it from other kinds of DNS records CoreDNS is also capable of serving inside the cluster, such as per Pod records for Headless Services.

The cluster.local segment is the cluster's own internal DNS domain suffix, configurable at cluster creation time but left at this default value in the overwhelming majority of real world clusters encountered in practice.

This predictability is genuinely valuable: given nothing more than a Service's name and namespace, its exact, fully qualified DNS name can always be constructed correctly, without needing to inspect the cluster or consult any documentation.

A Common Mistake: Forgetting the Namespace
blocks.text: A Common Mistake: Forgetting the Namespace

blocks.content: A common mistake is calling a Service using only its short name from a Pod running in a different namespace, then being confused when the DNS lookup fails or resolves to an entirely unexpected, unrelated Service.

As already covered in the previous topic, DNS search domain expansion only automatically appends the calling Pod's own namespace, never any other namespace. A Pod in namespace frontend cannot reach backend-service in namespace backend using the short name alone.

The correct fix, also already introduced in the previous topic, is to explicitly include the target namespace in the lookup, calling backend-service.backend rather than just backend-service, whenever the call genuinely crosses a namespace boundary.

This mistake is especially easy to make when an application is initially developed entirely within a single namespace and then later split across multiple namespaces, silently breaking cross namespace calls that previously worked by coincidence.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784642057452-918190247.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of forgetting the namespace across namespace boundaries

blocks.content: CoreDNS Configuration and Customization

CoreDNS's behavior is controlled by a configuration file called a Corefile, stored as a ConfigMap in the kube-system namespace, which defines exactly how it should handle different kinds of DNS queries.

Cluster administrators can customize this Corefile to add features such as custom DNS entries for external services, query forwarding rules for specific domains, or caching behavior tuned for a specific cluster's traffic patterns.

Most application developers never need to touch the Corefile directly, since the default configuration already correctly handles Service and Pod discovery out of the box, but knowing it exists is useful when diagnosing unusual DNS behavior.

Any change to the Corefile requires CoreDNS Pods to reload their configuration, and an incorrectly edited Corefile can break DNS resolution cluster wide, which is exactly why changes to it deserve careful, deliberate review.

blocks.title: Practical Note
blocks.content: The Corefile lives in a ConfigMap named coredns in the kube-system namespace. Treat edits to it with the same caution as any cluster wide infrastructure change.
CoreDNS Caching and Performance

CoreDNS caches DNS responses for a short, configurable duration by default, which meaningfully reduces load on the control plane by avoiding a fresh lookup against live cluster state for every single repeated DNS query from every Pod.

This caching introduces a small, deliberate window of potential staleness, typically measured in seconds, between a genuine change in a Service's backing Pods and every client's cached DNS answer reflecting that change.

In practice this window is short enough to be invisible for the overwhelming majority of applications, since the underlying Endpoints and kube proxy routing rules, covered in the next topic, update independently and far more quickly than the DNS cache window.

Understanding that this small caching layer exists is useful primarily for correctly interpreting DNS behavior during rapid testing or debugging sessions, where a just changed Service might briefly still resolve to its previous answer.
CoreDNS Resource Requests and Cluster Scale
blocks.text: CoreDNS Resource Requests and Cluster Scale

blocks.content: As a cluster grows larger, with more Pods performing more DNS queries, CoreDNS itself needs adequate CPU and memory resources allocated to it, exactly like any other application workload covered throughout this course.

An under resourced CoreDNS deployment in a large, busy cluster can become a genuine bottleneck, manifesting as intermittent DNS resolution failures or elevated latency that can be mistaken for an application level networking problem.

Cluster administrators typically scale the number of CoreDNS replicas horizontally as cluster size grows, using the exact same Deployment and Service mechanics already covered throughout this entire course for any other application.

This is a genuinely important operational fact for anyone running a large production cluster: CoreDNS is not a fixed, unlimited piece of magic infrastructure, but an ordinary workload that needs to be sized and monitored like any other.
DNS Policies at the Pod Level
blocks.text: DNS Policies at the Pod Level

blocks.content: Individual Pods can override their default DNS behavior using the dnsPolicy field in their spec, choosing between the cluster's default CoreDNS based resolution, the underlying node's own DNS configuration, or a fully custom configuration.

The default value, ClusterFirst, is what every example throughout this module has relied on implicitly, sending cluster internal names to CoreDNS while still allowing external, internet facing DNS names to be resolved normally as well.

Overriding this default is rare and reserved for specific edge cases, such as a Pod that genuinely needs to bypass CoreDNS entirely for a particular networking requirement, and should not be changed without a clear, specific reason.

Understanding that this override exists is useful primarily for recognizing it correctly during a manifest review, rather than being something most application manifests should ever need to touch directly.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: example-pod
spec:
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst  # the default, resolves cluster names via CoreDNS
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:v1

blocks.content: Diagnosing DNS Problems in Practice

When a Service appears correctly created but cannot be reached by name, checking whether CoreDNS itself is healthy, using kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns, should always be one of the very first diagnostic steps.

Running nslookup or dig directly from inside a Pod experiencing the problem, rather than from a machine outside the cluster, isolates whether the issue is genuinely DNS related or actually a separate networking or firewall problem.

Checking the calling Pod's own resolv.conf file, using kubectl exec into it and reading etc slash resolv.conf directly, confirms whether the Pod is actually configured to query CoreDNS in the first place, rather than some other DNS server.
CoreDNS Pod logs, viewed with kubectl logs, often reveal specific resolution errors directly, making them one of the fastest paths to understanding exactly why a particular DNS query is failing.
Using a Dedicated DNS Debugging Pod
blocks.text: Using a Dedicated DNS Debugging Pod

blocks.content: A genuinely useful diagnostic technique is running a small, disposable Pod, based on a minimal image containing standard networking tools, specifically to test DNS resolution from within the cluster without touching any real application Pod.

This dedicated debugging Pod can be started, used to run a series of nslookup and dig commands against various Service names, and then deleted immediately afterward, leaving no lasting footprint on the cluster.

This approach is often faster and cleaner than shelling into a real application Pod, since it avoids any risk of accidentally disrupting a production workload while investigating a DNS related problem.
Keeping the exact command for spinning up this kind of debugging Pod as a readily available reference is a small but genuinely valuable addition to any engineer's day to day operational toolkit.
kubectl run dns-debug --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- nslookup backend-service
DNS and Multi Container Pods

Every container within the same Pod shares the exact same network namespace, and therefore the exact same DNS configuration, meaning DNS resolution behaves identically regardless of which specific container within a Pod performs the lookup.

This shared behavior connects directly back to the multi container and sidecar patterns covered in the Pods module earlier in this course, where multiple containers cooperating within one Pod was established as a deliberate, common design pattern.

A sidecar container performing its own DNS lookups, such as a logging agent forwarding data to a Service by name, resolves that name using exactly the same CoreDNS mechanism as the primary application container beside it.

This consistency removes an entire category of potential confusion when debugging multi container Pods, since DNS behavior never needs to be reasoned about differently depending on which specific container within the Pod is involved.
Best Practices for Working With DNS
blocks.text: Best Practices for Working With DNS

blocks.content: Always use the short Service name within the same namespace and the fully qualified name across namespaces, treating the naming convention as a reliable, predictable fact rather than something to guess at each time.

Include a basic DNS health check, such as confirming CoreDNS Pods are running and ready, as part of any cluster wide health dashboard, since a DNS outage silently breaks nearly every other component's ability to communicate.

Avoid unnecessary custom Corefile changes unless there is a specific, well understood requirement, since the default configuration already correctly handles the overwhelming majority of real world use cases.

When diagnosing connectivity problems between components, check DNS resolution as an early step, before assuming the problem lies in application code or network policy, since a surprising number of connectivity issues trace back to DNS.

blocks.content: The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

CoreDNS is the concrete engine underneath every single DNS based Service lookup covered throughout this entire module, running as an ordinary, inspectable Kubernetes Deployment rather than as invisible, unexaminable magic.

The naming convention service-name.namespace-name.svc.cluster.local is entirely predictable and can always be constructed correctly from just a Service's name and namespace, without needing to inspect the live cluster.
The next topic, Endpoint, goes one level deeper still, covering exactly how Kubernetes tracks which specific Pod IP addresses a Service's name should actually resolve or route to at any given moment.

Keep CoreDNS's own health in mind as a standing operational concern. Every other piece of service discovery covered in this module depends entirely on it running correctly, continuously, in the background.

blocks.title: DNS In Full
points: CoreDNS is the internal DNS service running inside the cluster, deployed as an ordinary Deployment, and it powers every Service name resolution covered throughout this module.
Every Service automatically receives a predictable, fully qualified DNS name in the form service-name.namespace-name.svc.cluster.local.
Short names resolve automatically within the same namespace through DNS search domain expansion; cross namespace lookups require the explicit namespace suffix.
CoreDNS's own configuration lives in a Corefile ConfigMap in kube-system, and its health should be treated as a foundational cluster wide concern.
